scenes.headline: India gets richer. Women work less. Why?
scenes.subtext: India's female workforce participation is still below Pakistan's. And the women who do work are mostly unpaid.

stat.label: India's Female Labour Force Participation Rate (2023-24) — up from 23.3% in 2017-18, but quality matters more than the number

scenes.title: What is FLFPR — and why does quality matter more than the number?
scenes.body: FLFPR measures what percentage of working-age women are either employed or actively looking for work. India's number looks like it's rising — from 23.3% in 2017-18 to 41.7% in 2023-24. But here's the catch: almost all of that rise is rural women doing unpaid agricultural work or self-employment with zero job security. Real wage employment for women has actually shrunk.
scenes.analogy: Imagine a classroom where attendance has gone up — but half the students are just sitting in the back, not allowed to speak or be graded. The attendance number looks great. The learning is not happening.

zones.label: Crisis zone — women locked out of economy (India was here in 2017)
Distress participation — women work but in unpaid/informal roles (India today)
Structural inclusion — formal jobs, wages, security
Full participation — Economic Survey target of 55% by 2050

scenes.title: Why don't more women work in India?
scenes.intro: Six interlocking barriers keep women out of meaningful employment.

items.title: The care economy trap
items.detail: Indian women do 3-4 times more unpaid domestic work than men — childcare, cooking, eldercare. Until care work is shared or professionalised, women's time for paid work stays limited.
items.stat: 31% of women cite commuting as a barrier — World Bank 2021

items.title: Pink collarization — sorted into low-paying jobs
items.detail: Pink collar jobs are occupations dominated by women — nursing, teaching, domestic work. These jobs are systematically underpaid compared to male-dominated roles requiring similar skills.
items.stat: Gender pay gap: women earn ₹19,879/month vs men's ₹26,105 in urban areas

items.title: The education-employment disconnect
items.detail: Women now make up 43% of STEM graduates — but only 27% of the STEM workforce. Education is happening; employment is not following.

items.title: Urban safety and commute barrier
items.detail: In cities where the best jobs are, women face unsafe transport, harassment, and lack of affordable housing. Economic Survey 2025-26 specifically called out mobility and housing as structural barriers.
items.stat: Tamil Nadu's 'Thozhi Hostels' and Sakhi Niwas scheme are government responses

items.title: The U-curve paradox (Claudia Goldin, Nobel 2023)
items.detail: FLFPR actually drops during early industrialisation — women leave agriculture but lack permission or skills for factory work — and rises again only when services and education expand. India is mid-curve right now.

items.title: The motherhood penalty
items.detail: Women's careers take a permanent hit after having children — they exit the workforce, take breaks, or shift to part-time work. Men's careers don't.
items.stat: Women enter formal workforce at age 39 on average vs men at 32 — McKinsey 2025

scenes.title: The rising FLFPR — good news or statistical illusion?

left_items.label: Numbers are rising
left_items.detail: FLFPR went from 23.3% to 41.7% in 6 years — fastest rise in decades

left_items.label: Rural entrepreneurship growing
left_items.detail: Women head 26.2% of proprietary establishments — up from 24.2% in two years

left_items.label: Government schemes expanding
left_items.detail: Mudra loans, SHG networks, Lakhpati Didi target — women-led rural economy is policy priority

right_items.label: Rise is mostly unpaid work
right_items.detail: The increase is in agriculture and self-employment — not wage jobs with security or benefits

right_items.label: Still below global average
right_items.detail: Global female FLFPR average is 47.2%. India at 41.7% — quality-adjusted, even lower

right_items.label: Organised sector shrinking for women
right_items.detail: Women's share in regular salaried, organised sector jobs has actually declined

scenes.officer_framing: India's rising FLFPR is real but fragile — it reflects distress participation more than genuine economic inclusion. The goal isn't more women working; it's more women in dignified, secure, well-paid work.

scenes.title: The big picture — what's at stake
scenes.body: Economic Survey 2025-26 made a stark projection: raising women's workforce participation to 55% by 2050 is critical for India to sustain high GDP growth. McKinsey estimated that reaching male participation levels could increase India's GDP by over 25%.

key_numbers.label: Potential GDP increase if women reach male FLFPR levels — McKinsey
India's rank in WEF Global Gender Gap Report 2025
FLFPR target for India by 2050 — Economic Survey 2025-26
More unpaid domestic work done by Indian women vs men

scenes.title: Use this in SSB
scenes.pi_question: Why is India's female workforce participation so low despite rising education levels?
scenes.gd_line: India's rising FLFPR looks encouraging on paper, but most of the increase is in unpaid agricultural work — not formal employment. The real challenge is not getting women to work more, but ensuring that when they work, it is dignified, safe, and fairly compensated.
lecturette_structure: Open: India grows richer — yet women are working less in quality jobs. The workforce paradox.
Define: FLFPR — what it measures, India's number vs global average of 47.2%
Causes: Pink collarization, care economy trap, U-curve, motherhood penalty — pick 2-3
Two sides: Numbers rising vs quality declining — the statistical illusion problem
Close: Economic Survey's 55% by 2050 target — this is a GDP strategy, not just a gender policy
scenes.pi_answer: Sir, India's female workforce participation presents a paradox — participation numbers are rising, but quality is declining. Most of the increase is in rural unpaid agricultural work, not formal wage employment. The root causes are interconnected: pink collarization steers women into low-paying sectors, the care economy burden falls disproportionately on women, and urban safety barriers prevent access to better jobs. The goal must shift from participation to meaningful participation.
scenes.one_liner: It's not enough for women to work — they must be allowed to earn, advance, and lead.

questions.q: India's FLFPR rose from 23.3% to 41.7% in 6 years. A GD participant says this proves women's empowerment is succeeding. Your response?
options: Agree — rising numbers always mean progress
Partially — the rise is real but most gains are in unpaid rural work, not formal employment. True empowerment requires quality jobs, not just participation numbers.
Disagree — the numbers are completely fake
questions.explanation: The nuanced answer shows analytical depth — you understand both the data and its limitations. That's the OLQ thinking boards look for.

options: The pattern of women being concentrated in certain occupations — nursing, teaching, domestic work — that are systematically underpaid relative to their skill requirements
The gender pay gap in the IT sector
questions.explanation: Pink collar jobs are real occupations, not a government policy. They're underpaid not because they're unskilled, but because they're feminised — society values them less.
